arguments.heading: Argument analysis: April 20, 2026 session
paragraphs: This was the only argument session in the approved record. It was not a reargument. Both sides appeared, and the Chief Justice called the case.

The challenger, Daniel Geyser, asked the Court to limit disgorgement to restoring the status quo and compensating injured investors. He argued it cannot be a penalty or deterrent. He asked the Court to require proof of investor economic harm. He suggested civil penalties or private suits where distribution is hard.

The government, through Malcolm Stewart, asked the Court to uphold disgorgement as a profits-based remedy. It argued the challenger would transform it into a compensatory, loss-measured remedy. It said the challenger must prevail on both narrowing victims and resolving Liu's Treasury question. It defended keeping funds for deterrence.

The justices tested several assumptions. Justice Thomas tested whether disgorgement is still equitable after the statutory move. Justice Alito tested whether the SEC holds a substantive entitlement to profits. Justice Sotomayor tested measurement, the provable-loss cap, and the Seventh Amendment problem with deterrence-only keeping. Justice Gorsuch tested net profits, causation, and whether investor injury can be resolved without deciding the funds-keeping scope. Justice Kagan tested which subsection gives the government its best argument. Justice Jackson tested jury trial rights.

The challenger conceded no double recovery of damages and disgorgement for the same injury, and confirmed the provable-loss cap. The government conceded causation between unjust enrichment and the defendant's actions, and confirmed net profits only. It also said the Court could avoid deciding the funds-keeping scope.
No reargument session appears in the approved record, so nothing changed or was revisited on reargument.

case.dek: The Supreme Court heard one side-by-side debate about how far the SEC's disgorgement power reaches.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case asks what disgorgement means. Disgorgement is when a court orders someone who broke securities rules to give up profits they made from the wrongdoing. The question is whether that money must go to injured investors, or whether the government can keep it.
Daniel Geyser argued for the person challenging the SEC. Malcolm Stewart argued for the government. The Chief Justice called the case, and the argument started at 10:05 in the morning.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: The challenger wants the Court to limit disgorgement. He asks the Court to treat it as a way to restore the status quo and compensate injured investors, not as a way to punish. He also wants the SEC to prove investors suffered economic harm before seeking disgorgement.

The government wants broader freedom. It argues disgorgement is a profits-based remedy, measured by the wrongdoer's gains rather than victims' losses. It says the government can keep funds even when distribution to investors is difficult, and that this serves deterrence.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: The challenger's core argument relies on an earlier case called Liu. He says Congress wrote the disgorgement rule against Liu's backdrop, pairing disgorgement with penalties as separate remedies. He warns that reading disgorgement as mere deprivation would erase the line between disgorgement and civil penalties.

He also paints the government's view harshly. He says the government's position lets disgorgement act like a penalty, focused on taking money away and deterrence, with no remedial purpose or return of funds to investors.
He made one concession. He agreed a party cannot recover both damages and disgorgement for the same injury. He also confirmed disgorgement cannot exceed provable loss.

The government pushed back on Liu. It says Liu did not define the statutory term disgorgement, because that word did not even appear in the older provision. Liu spoke to traditional equitable practice, not to the word's meaning.

The government also says the challenger wants to shrink who counts as a victim. The same side also seeks to force the Court to answer Liu's open question about routing undistributed funds to the Treasury. It says the challenger must win both points to prevail.

On jury trials, the government's position is that civil penalties require a jury, but disgorgement does not. It also says its position does not depend on whether the remedy is legal or equitable; that status may affect jury rights but not whether the remedy is available.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Thomas asked the challenger to explain the difference between disgorgement and compensatory damages. The challenger answered that disgorgement identifies an asset that rightfully belongs to someone else, while damages make an injured party whole.
Justice Thomas also asked whether disgorgement is still equitable after Congress moved it into a section with a different time limit. The challenger answered that it remains equitable.

Justice Sotomayor pressed hard on measurement. She asked whether disgorgement should be measured by the wrongdoer's profits rather than victims' losses, and whether the maximum disgorgement equals only provable loss. The challenger confirmed the cap and said wrongful profits are part of the equation.

Justice Alito asked why, if disgorgement stays equitable, the SEC would not hold a substantive entitlement to profits, like an accounting for profits. The challenger answered that the SEC is not the victim, and that reading disgorgement as mere deprivation would collapse the statutory distinction with civil penalties.

Justice Kagan asked the government why one statutory subsection gives it a better argument than another. Justice Gorsuch asked the government to confirm the provision covers net profits only, and that unjust enrichment must be causally connected to the defendant's actions. The government agreed on causation and confirmed net profits only.
Justice Jackson asked whether a jury trial is required for civil penalties but not for disgorgement. The government answered yes, consistent with its stated position.

Justice Sotomayor also tested the government's deterrence theory. She asked what legally protected right the government vindicates if it keeps the money, and whether keeping money for deterrence alone creates a Seventh Amendment problem. The Seventh Amendment is the constitutional guarantee of jury trials in certain money-award cases. The government answered that keeping funds serves the public interest in depriving unlawful profits.

Justice Gorsuch asked whether the Court could resolve whether investor injury must be shown without deciding the scope of the provision about keeping funds. The government answered that the Court could avoid deciding that scope.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The stakes turn on where disgorged money goes. The government said distribution to investors matters under one subsection but not under the others. The challenger said investors may have suffered a violation of legal interests but hold no legal right to the proceeds.

The challenger also argued the government could use civil penalties or private suits if distributing money is hard. The government countered that equitable remedies like injunctions serve deterrence, and that one Supreme Court case approved disgorgement exceeding victim loss.
